notes:
Area under a curve

  • Area bounded by $y=f(x)$, the x-axis, and lines $x=a,x=b$ (with $f(x)\ge0$): $A=\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
  • If part of the curve lies below the x-axis, take the absolute value of that part's integral before adding (area is always positive).
  • Area bounded by $x=g(y)$, y-axis, and $y=c,y=d$: $A=\displaystyle\int_c^d g(y)\,dy$.

Area between two curves

  • If $f(x)\ge g(x)$ on $[a,b]$: $A=\displaystyle\int_a^b [f(x)-g(x)]\,dx$.
  • Always find intersection points first (solve $f(x)=g(x)$) to get correct limits.

Standard curves & areas

CurveRegion / Area
Circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$Full area $=\pi a^2$; area in first quadrant $=\pi a^2/4$
Ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$Full area $=\pi ab$
Parabola $y^2=4ax$ and line $x=a$Area $=\dfrac{8a^2}{3}$ (both sides of axis)
Line $y=mx$ and parabola $y=x^2$Find intersections, integrate (line $-$ parabola)

Useful integrals for area problems

  • $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+\dfrac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{a}+C$.
  • $\displaystyle\int_0^a\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{\pi a^2}{4}$ (quarter circle area, a quick shortcut).
  • Power rule: $\displaystyle\int x^n\,dx=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$ ($n\ne-1$).

Method / steps

  • 1. Sketch (or mentally visualise) the region. 2. Identify boundaries and points of intersection. 3. Decide whether to integrate w.r.t. $x$ or $y$ (whichever gives simpler limits/integrand). 4. Set up the definite integral of (upper $-$ lower) or (right $-$ left). 5. Evaluate.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 1-2 questions from this chapter, most often the area under a simple parabola/line, the standard circle-quadrant area, or area between a line and a parabola. Memorising the ready-made results for circle, ellipse and parabola areas saves valuable time versus deriving them from scratch.

questions.q: The area bounded by the curve $y=x^2$, the x-axis and the lines $x=0,x=2$ is
questions.trick: $\int_a^b f(x)dx$ with $f=x^2$ gives the area directly.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=x$, the x-axis and $x=0,x=4$ is
questions.trick: $y=x$ is a line: check $\frac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$ against the integral.

questions.q: The area of the circle $x^2+y^2=16$ lying in the first quadrant is
questions.explanation: Full circle area $=\pi r^2=16\pi$; first quadrant is a quarter: $16\pi/4=4\pi$.
questions.trick: Quadrant of a circle is always $\pi r^2/4$ — no integration needed.

questions.q: The area enclosed by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}=1$ is
questions.trick: Full ellipse area $=\pi ab$; memorise it, skip integration.

questions.q: The area between the parabola $y^2=4x$ and the line $x=4$ (both sides of the x-axis) is
questions.trick: $y^2=4ax$ area: double the one-sided integral by symmetry about the x-axis.

questions.q: The area bounded by $y=\sin x$ and the x-axis between $x=0$ and $x=\pi$ is
questions.trick: $\sin x$ stays positive on $[0,\pi]$, so integrate directly — no splitting needed.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=x^2$ and $y=x$ is
questions.trick: Between two curves: find intersections first, then $\int(\text{top}-\text{bottom})$.

questions.q: The area under the curve $y=\sqrt{4-x^2}$ from $x=0$ to $x=2$ (a quarter circle of radius 2) is
questions.trick: Quarter-circle shortcut: $\pi r^2/4$, here with $r=2$.

questions.q: The area bounded by the curve $y=e^x$, the x-axis, and the lines $x=0,x=1$ is
questions.trick: $\int e^x=e^x$: just plug in the limits and subtract.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y^2=x$, the y-axis, and the lines $y=0,y=3$ is
questions.trick: Bounded by the y-axis? Integrate w.r.t. $y$ instead of $x$.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the line $y=3x+2$, the x-axis and the lines $x=-1,x=1$ is
questions.explanation: The line crosses the x-axis at $x=-2/3$. For $x\in[-1,-2/3]$, $y<0$, giving $\left|\int_{-1}^{-2/3}(3x+2)dx\right|=\dfrac16$; for $x\in[-2/3,1]$, $y>0$, giving $\int_{-2/3}^{1}(3x+2)dx=\dfrac{25}{6}$. Total area $=\dfrac16+\dfrac{25}{6}=\dfrac{26}{6}=\dfrac{13}{3}$.
questions.trick: Line crosses the axis: split at the root, take $|{\cdot}|$ of each piece, add.

questions.q: The area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by $y^2=4x$, $x=1$ and $x=4$ is
questions.trick: $\sqrt{4x}$ integral: pull out the constant, use the $x^{3/2}$ power rule.

questions.q: The area of the smaller region bounded by the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ and the line $x=1$ (to the right of the line, inside the circle) is
questions.trick: Circular segment $=2\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}dx$ using the standard antiderivative formula.

questions.q: For a region where the curve lies below the x-axis over $[a,b]$, the area (a positive quantity) is given by
questions.explanation: Since $f(x)<0$ there, the plain integral is negative; taking its absolute value gives the (positive) area.
questions.trick: Absolute value converts a negative below-axis integral into true positive area.

questions.q: The area bounded by $y=\cos x$, the x-axis, $x=0$ and $x=\pi/2$ is
questions.trick: $\int\cos x=\sin x$: plug in limits directly.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=x^3$, the x-axis, and $x=-1,x=1$ is
questions.explanation: By symmetry the areas on either side are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign; total area (using absolute values) $=2\int_0^1x^3dx=2\times\dfrac14=\dfrac12$ (the plain integral over $[-1,1]$ would wrongly give 0).
questions.trick: Odd function about the x-axis flips sign — double one side, never subtract across it.

questions.q: The area enclosed between the parabola $y=x^2$ and the line $y=4$ is
questions.trick: Curve vs. horizontal line: integrate (line$-$curve) between the two intersection x-values.

questions.q: To find the area between two curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ over $[a,b]$ where they cross at an interior point, the correct approach is to
options: split the interval at the crossing point and integrate $|f-g|$ on each part
questions.explanation: Since which function is on top switches at the crossing point, the interval must be split there and the areas added, each taken as a positive quantity.
questions.trick: Curves crossing mid-interval: split there, or the areas wrongly cancel.

questions.q: The area bounded by the curve $y=\sqrt x$, the x-axis and the ordinates $x=0,x=9$ is
questions.trick: $\int\sqrt x\,dx=\tfrac23x^{3/2}$ — apply the power rule to the fractional exponent.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=4-x^2$ and the x-axis is
questions.trick: Symmetric parabola: double the integral from $0$ to the root instead of the full range.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=3x^2$, the x-axis and the lines $x=1,x=2$ is
questions.trick: $\int 3x^2=x^3$: plug in limits, subtract the cubes.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=x+2$, the x-axis and the lines $x=-1,x=1$ is
questions.trick: Check the sign first: if $f(x)>0$ throughout, integrate directly, no splitting.

questions.q: The area of the circle $x^2+y^2=9$ lying in the second quadrant is
questions.explanation: Full circle area $=\pi(3)^2=9\pi$; a quadrant is one-fourth of this, $\dfrac{9\pi}{4}$.
questions.trick: Any quadrant of a circle is exactly $\tfrac14$ of $\pi r^2$.

questions.q: The area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=1$ and the coordinate axes is
questions.explanation: Full ellipse area $=\pi ab=\pi(4)(3)=12\pi$; the first-quadrant quarter is $3\pi$.
questions.trick: Quarter-ellipse $=\tfrac14\pi ab$, the same shortcut as for a circle.

questions.q: The area bounded by $y=|x|$, the x-axis and the lines $x=-2,x=2$ is
questions.explanation: The region is two right triangles each of area $\dfrac12(2)(2)=2$, giving a total of $4$.
questions.trick: $|x|$ bounded region = two identical right triangles; skip integration.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=5$, the x-axis and the lines $x=0,x=3$ is
questions.explanation: This is a rectangle of width 3 and height 5, so $A=\int_0^3 5\,dx=15$.
questions.trick: Constant $y=c$ over $[a,b]$ is just a rectangle: area $=c(b-a)$.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=x$, the x-axis and the lines $x=2,x=5$ is
questions.trick: $\int x\,dx=x^2/2$: plug in limits and subtract.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the parabolas $y=x^2$ and $y=4x-x^2$ is
questions.trick: Two parabolas: equate to find intersections, then $\int(\text{upper}-\text{lower})$.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the parabolas $y^2=4x$ and $x^2=4y$ is
questions.trick: Symmetric parabolas about $y=x$: find intersections, integrate $\left(2\sqrt x-\tfrac{x^2}{4}\right)$.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=x^3$, the x-axis and the lines $x=1,x=2$ is
questions.trick: $\int x^3=x^4/4$: plug in limits, subtract.

questions.q: The area bounded by $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$, the x-axis and the lines $x=1,x=e$ is
questions.trick: $\int(1/x)dx=\ln x$: limits $1$ to $e$ always give exactly $1$.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=4-x^2$ and the line $y=x+2$ is
questions.trick: Line vs. parabola: solve the intersection quadratic, integrate (line$-$parabola).

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=\sqrt x$ and $y=x$ between $x=0$ and $x=1$ is
questions.trick: Compare $\sqrt x$ and $x$ on $[0,1]$: $\sqrt x$ is always on top.

questions.q: The area of the triangular region in the first quadrant bounded by $y=4-x$ and the coordinate axes is
questions.trick: Line $+$ axes forms a right triangle — check $\tfrac12\text{base}\times\text{height}$ before integrating.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=x^2-4$ and the x-axis between $x=-2$ and $x=2$ is
questions.trick: Curve dips below the axis: take $|\int|$, don't report the negative raw value.

questions.q: The smaller area between the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{4}+y^2=1$ and the line $\dfrac{x}{2}+y=1$ (in the first quadrant) is
questions.explanation: Quarter-ellipse area $=\dfrac{\pi(2)(1)}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; the triangle formed by the chord and axes has area $\dfrac12(2)(1)=1$. The region between the arc and the chord is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}-1$.
questions.trick: Segment between an ellipse arc and its chord $=$ quarter ellipse $-$ triangle.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the parabola $y^2=4ax$ and its latus rectum ($x=a$) is
questions.trick: Latus-rectum area for $y^2=4ax$ is the standard $\tfrac{8a^2}{3}$ — memorise it.

questions.q: Using integration, the area of the triangle with vertices $(2,0)$, $(4,5)$ and $(6,3)$ is
questions.explanation: Summing the integrals of the three side-lines (or using $\tfrac12|x_1(y_2-y_3)+x_2(y_3-y_1)+x_3(y_1-y_2)|$) gives $\tfrac12|2(2)+4(3)+6(-5)|=\tfrac12(14)=7$.
questions.trick: Triangle area via vertices: $\tfrac12|x_1(y_2-y_3)+x_2(y_3-y_1)+x_3(y_1-y_2)|$ beats 3 integrals.

questions.q: The area of the region $\{(x,y): x^2+y^2\le4,\ x+y\ge2\}$ is
questions.explanation: This is the minor segment cut off by the chord $x+y=2$: quarter-circle area $\pi$ minus the right triangle of area $2$ (vertices $(0,0),(2,0),(0,2)$), giving $\pi-2$.
questions.trick: Region above a chord inside a circle $=$ quarter circle $-$ chord's triangle.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by $y=x^2$ and $y=|x|$ for $-1\le x\le1$ is
questions.trick: By symmetry compute for $x\ge0$ and double: check which curve sits on top.
